# --description--

A typical use of `guard let` is validating a function's input at the top and returning a fallback value when it is missing:
```swift
func length(of text: String?) -> Int {
    guard let text = text else { return 0 }
    return text.count
}
```

# --instructions--

Write a function `half` that takes an `Int?` (omit the argument label) and returns the number divided by `2`, or `-1` when the optional is `nil`.
Use `guard let`

# --before-seed--

```swift
// DO NOT EDIT FROM HERE
import Foundation

var _testCount = 0
var _testFailedCount = 0
func tryCatch(_ assertion: Bool) {
    _testCount += 1
    if !assertion {
        _testFailedCount += 1
        print("Test Case '--err-t\(_testCount)--' failed")
    }
}
// DO NOT EDIT UNTIL HERE
```

# --asserts--

`half(10)` must return `5`

```swift
tryCatch(half(10) == 5)
```

`half(7)` must return `3`

```swift
tryCatch(half(7) == 3)
```

`half(nil)` must return `-1`

```swift
tryCatch(half(nil) == -1)
```

# --after-asserts--

```swift
print("Executed \(_testCount) tests, with \(_testFailedCount) failures")
```

# --solutions--

```swift
func half(_ number: Int?) -> Int {
    guard let number = number else { return -1 }
    return number / 2
}
```
